canonicalExplanation.summary: A machine-learning project should start with a **problem statement**, not a model. Pin down: the **prediction unit** (one ticket? one customer per month?), the **target** and **when** it's known versus when you predict, **who uses** the prediction and **what action** it enables, the **population** it applies to, a simple **baseline** to beat, the **costs of each error type** (missing an urgent case vs. wasting a specialist's time), **non-goals** (what the system will not do) and a **measurable success criterion**. Grabbing whatever label column exists and maximising accuracy often produces a model that's accurate at something nobody needs, or that uses information not available at prediction time.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner finds a column called resolved_by_specialist in old support data and trains a model with 94% accuracy. Nobody can use it: the column is filled in after the ticket closes, the model used the closing notes to predict it, and 94% equals always guessing "no". A support triage project predicts whether a ticket needs specialist review at intake, compares a rules baseline, and measures missed urgent cases plus reviewer workload. In this lesson you'll write a measurable ML problem statement with non-goals and baseline.

```predict
{"question": "A model predicts a label with 94% accuracy. What should you check first?", "options": ["Which algorithm was used", "What a trivial baseline scores, and whether the inputs exist at prediction time"], "answer": 1, "why": "Accuracy without a baseline and timing check means little."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Debugger and final project**, **Problem and environment characteristics** and **Inputs, outputs and constraints** (defining inputs and outputs precisely).

sections.heading: The model: a problem card before any model
sections.body:
```python
problem = {
    "unit": "one support ticket",           # what one prediction is about.
    "predict_at": "ticket creation (title, body, product, customer tier only)",
    "target": "needs specialist review (decided by lead within 48h)",
    "user_action": "route to specialist queue immediately",
    "population": "English tickets for products A and B",
    # Beat this simple rule first.
    "baseline": "rule: tier == 'enterprise' or 'outage' in title",
    "error_costs": "missed urgent ticket >> extra specialist review",
    "success": "catch >= 90% of urgent tickets with <= 30% more specialist load",
    # Out of scope on purpose.
    "non_goals": ["auto-reply to customers", "rank staff performance"],
}
missing = [k for k in ("unit", "predict_at", "target", "baseline", "success", "non_goals") if not problem.get(k)]
print("complete" if not missing else missing)     # complete
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why write non-goals?", "answer": "They stop scope creep and misuse. If the model is later proposed for ranking staff, the card shows it was never designed or evaluated for that."}
```

examples.title: Triage for specialist support tickets
examples.situation: A support triage project predicts whether a ticket needs specialist review at intake, compares a rules baseline, and measures missed urgent cases plus reviewer workload.
walkthrough: **Predicts whether a ticket needs specialist review at intake:** only fields available at creation are allowed.
**Compares a rules baseline:** enterprise tier or outage in the title.
**Measures missed urgent cases plus reviewer workload:** we check at least 90% of urgent tickets are caught with at most 30% more load.
examples.result: The team knows exactly what success means before training anything.

examples.title: The 94% model nobody could use
examples.situation: A model predicted resolved_by_specialist with 94% accuracy using closing notes written after resolution.
walkthrough: The target and inputs were only known after the ticket closed.
Redefine prediction time as ticket creation and drop later fields.
Compare with the always-no baseline and the rules baseline.
examples.result: The project measures a usable prediction against honest baselines.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Choosing an available target column and maximizing its test accuracy is enough to define a useful ML problem.
misconceptions.correction: A useful problem defines the unit, timing, user action, baseline, error costs, success and non-goals before choosing a target or model.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The 94% model nobody could use", what was wrong with the timing?

analogy.example: A problem card is like **a brief for an architect**. "Build something with nice rooms" gets a lovely house in the wrong place. A good brief says **who lives there, what they do, the budget, what's off-limits, and how you'll judge success**. Only then does choosing materials (the model) make sense.
limitations: A baseline is the existing house you must beat.
Error costs are which mistakes are expensive to fix.

recap.summary: To write a measurable ML problem statement with non-goals and baseline, define the prediction unit and time, the target, the user and action, the population, a simple baseline, error costs and a measurable success criterion, and list what the system will not do.
